records.text: Milton Mukai Accompanied his parents and grandmother Kuni when the Mukai family self-exiled from Vashon Island to Dead Ox Flat, Oregon, in March 1942. One of the four Mukai family members who avoided internment. historical figure

records.title: John Cherberg
records.text: John Cherberg Made the procedural ruling on March 12, 1959, that effectively killed the most serious Vashon Island bridge proposal in history. Ruled that the House bill had broadened the original scope and must return to committee. A vote to override his ruling failed 21 to 28, and the bridge was never built. government official

records.title: Fred Eernisse
records.text: Fred Eernisse Co-founded the Vashon Arts League in 1949 with Norman Edson and Art Hansen, which became the oldest private nonprofit community arts organization in Washington State. The organization eventually grew into Vashon Center for the Arts. artist

records.title: Norman Edson
records.text: Norman Edson Co-founded the Vashon Arts League in 1949, showing art created by islanders. The organization received 501(c)(3) status in 1966 and became the island's largest nonprofit arts institution. artist

records.title: Art Hansen
records.text: Art Hansen Co-founded the Vashon Arts League in 1949 with Fred Eernisse and Norman Edson, establishing the institutional foundation for the island's arts community. artist

records.title: Shirley Speidel
records.text: Shirley Speidel Helped revitalize the Vashon arts organization, finding a permanent home in the old Boy Scout Cabin at Ober Park. Instrumental in the organization receiving its 501(c)(3) nonprofit status in 1966 as Vashon Associated Arts. community leader

records.title: Tony Grant
records.text: Tony Grant A 17-year-old who was held down by three loggers who forcibly cut his hair during the cultural tensions surrounding the counterculture influx to Vashon Island around 1970. The incident exemplified the friction between long-time residents and the incoming counterculture movement. logger

records.title: Bill Kirschner
records.text: Bill Kirschner University of Washington engineering graduate who pioneered fiberglass ski technology. Experimented in his grandfather Otto's garage on Vashon Island before perfecting a wet-wrap fiberglass process in 1961. Co-founded K2 Corporation with his brother Don in 1962. The company became the island's largest private employer with approximately 750 workers at its peak. business owner

records.title: Don Kirschner
records.text: Don Kirschner Co-founded K2 Corporation on Vashon Island with his brother Bill in 1962, named for both the world's second-highest mountain and the two Kirschner brothers. The company revolutionized the ski industry with fiberglass technology. business owner

records.title: Otto Kirschner
records.text: Otto Kirschner His garage on Vashon Island served as the original workshop where Bill Kirschner experimented with fiberglass ski prototypes in the 1950s, leading to the founding of K2 Corporation. historical figure

records.title: Jim Stewart
records.text: Jim Stewart Moved his coffee roasting operation to Vashon Island in 1982, purchasing a historic building in the town of Vashon. After winning a regional tasting competition, the company changed its name from Stewart Brothers Coffee to Seattle's Best Coffee. Starbucks acquired SBC in 2003 and closed the Vashon facility. The building was later reopened as The Vashon Island Coffee Roasterie. business owner

records.title: Lawrence Matsuda
records.text: Lawrence Matsuda Collaborated with artist Roger Shimomura on the "Nisei Trilogy," a collaborative artwork depicting the Japanese American wartime experience, which is on permanent display in the Mukai house on Vashon Island. artist

records.title: Roger Shimomura
records.text: Roger Shimomura Collaborated with poet Lawrence Matsuda on the "Nisei Trilogy," a collaborative artwork depicting the Japanese American wartime experience, on permanent display at Mukai Farm and Garden on Vashon Island. artist

records.title: Berkeley Breathed
records.text: Berkeley Breathed Wrote the children's book "Red Ranger Came Calling," inspired by Vashon Island's iconic "Bike in the Tree" landmark -- a bicycle gradually absorbed by a growing fir tree since the 1950s. writer

records.title: Don Puz
records.text: Don Puz Original owner of the red bicycle that became the iconic "Bike in the Tree" landmark. After a devastating house fire killed his father in 1954, neighbors donated the bicycle to young Don. He left it leaning against a small fir tree, which gradually grew around it over the decades. historical figure

records.title: Jeff Ammon
records.text: Jeff Ammon Maintained the "Bike in the Tree" landmark by replacing handlebars and wheels when vandals stripped them, helping preserve one of the island's most quirky and beloved attractions. historical figure

records.title: Sharon Nelson
records.text: Sharon Nelson Founded Preserve Our Islands, the grassroots organization that led the 13-year fight against Glacier Northwest's proposed gravel mine expansion on Maury Island. The battle ended in 2010 when King County purchased the 200-acre site for $36 million, creating a new county park. historical figure

records.title: Dow Constantine
records.text: Dow Constantine Completed the purchase of the Glacier Northwest gravel mine site on Maury Island on December 30, 2010, for $36 million. The 200-acre parcel became a county park, protecting a mile of shoreline and over 200 acres of madrone forest. historical figure

records.title: Jim Bristow
records.text: Jim Bristow Led the Vashon Medical Reserve Corps (VMRC) in a volunteer-driven pandemic response that achieved the lowest COVID-19 case rate in King County. The program delivered over 19,000 vaccine doses, conducted 7,500+ PCR tests, and was recognized by the New York Times as a model for rural communities. community leader

records.title: Glenda Pearson
records.text: Glenda Pearson Longtime Vashon Island community organizer and advocate for rural character preservation. Active in land use planning debates that shaped the island's identity as a haven for artists and small-scale agriculture rather than suburban development. community leader

records.title: Betty MacDonald
records.text: Betty MacDonald Author of 'The Egg and I' (1945), a humorous memoir of rural life that became a bestseller and inspired the Ma and Pa Kettle film series. While set on the Olympic Peninsula, MacDonald later lived on Vashon Island with her second husband, Donald MacDonald, in the 1940s-50s. Her presence contributed to Vashon's literary reputation. writer

records.title: Jean Findlay
records.text: Jean Findlay Founding member of the Vashon-Maury Island Heritage Association (later Vashon Heritage Museum). Instrumental in preserving island historical records, oral histories, and artifacts. Led early efforts to document pioneer-era structures before they were lost. community leader

records.title: Bruce Haulman
records.text: Bruce Haulman Vashon Island's preeminent modern historian and author. Creator of vashonhistory.com, the most comprehensive online resource for island history. Author of multiple books on Vashon history and regular columnist for the Vashon-Maury Island Beachcomber. His work has made island history accessible to researchers and the general public. historian

records.title: Rayna Holtz
records.text: Rayna Holtz Pioneer of the organic farming movement on Vashon Island. Helped establish the Vashon Island Growers Association and the Saturday Farmers Market, which became central to the island's identity as an organic agriculture community. Part of the back-to-the-land movement that drew young farmers to the island in the 1970s-80s. farmer

records.title: John de Groen
records.text: John de Groen Co-founder and early leader of K2 Corporation alongside the Kirschner family. Helped transform K2 from a small island ski manufacturer into a major sporting goods company. K2 became Vashon's largest employer and its economic anchor for decades. business owner

records.title: Norie Sato
records.text: Norie Sato Japanese American artist based on Vashon Island, known for large-scale public art installations throughout the Pacific Northwest. Her work explores themes of memory, landscape, and cultural identity. Recipient of numerous public art commissions including works for Sound Transit and the Seattle Art Museum. artist

records.title: Kara Jones
records.text: Kara Jones Vashon Island poet and publisher. Founded Soulstice Press, a small literary press based on the island. Representative of the vibrant independent publishing and poetry community that flourished on Vashon from the 1990s onward. artist

records.title: Henning Sehmsdorf
records.text: Henning Sehmsdorf Professor Emeritus at University of Washington and Vashon Island organic farmer. Co-founded the S&S Homestead Farm on Vashon, a model for sustainable biodynamic agriculture. Author of works on sustainable farming practices. His farm became an educational center for regenerative agriculture. educator

records.title: Elizabeth Simpson
records.text: Elizabeth Simpson Co-founder of S&S Homestead Farm on Vashon Island with Henning Sehmsdorf. Together they developed one of the Pacific Northwest's premier demonstrations of biodynamic and sustainable farming practices, hosting workshops and educational programs for decades. educator

records.title: Captain Alexander M. Peabody
records.text: Captain Alexander M. Peabody President of the Black Ball Line (Puget Sound Navigation Company), which operated ferry service to Vashon Island before state takeover. His contentious relationship with the Washington Toll Bridge Authority over fares and subsidies led to the dramatic 1951 state purchase of the Black Ball fleet, creating Washington State Ferries. business owner

records.title: Alex Anderson
records.text: Alex Anderson Chairman of the Vashon Island anti-bridge committee in the late 1950s. Led the successful grassroots campaign that defeated the 1959 proposal to build a bridge connecting Vashon to the mainland. The campaign's victory preserved the island's rural character and ferry-dependent identity. community leader

records.title: Leschi's Wife (Mary)
records.text: Leschi's Wife (Mary) Wife of Chief Leschi of the Nisqually. During the Puget Sound War, she and other family members were among those displaced by the conflict. Her story represents the broader experience of indigenous women and families during the treaty era and forced relocations. historical figure

records.title: William Tolmie
records.text: William Tolmie Chief Factor at the Hudson's Bay Company's Fort Nisqually from 1843. Managed the Puget Sound Agricultural Company, which ran livestock operations that competed with American settlers for land. His presence and the HBC's claims complicated early American settlement patterns around Vashon Island. business owner

records.title: Lucy Gerand
records.text: Lucy Gerand Puyallup woman and vital historical witness to pre-settlement Vashon Island life. Interviewed by anthropologist T.T. Waterman in the 1920s, she provided detailed accounts of traditional place names, village sites, and seasonal resource gathering patterns of the sx̌ʷəbabš (S'Homamish) people on Vashon and Maury Islands. Her testimony remains one of the most important primary sources for understanding indigenous lifeways on the island. indigenous leader

records.title: Captain Gertrude Wiman
records.text: Captain Gertrude Wiman First woman licensed as a steamship pilot on Puget Sound, earning her license around 1907. Commanded vessels on the Mosquito Fleet routes that served Vashon Island, breaking gender barriers in the maritime industry at a time when women captains were virtually unheard of. Her achievement reflected the independent spirit of island communities that depended on these small ferry operators. historical figure

records.title: Marjorie Rose Stanley
records.text: Marjorie Rose Stanley Vashon Island historian who spent over 60 years documenting island history. Published the first 'History of Vashon Island' in 1926 and later serialized an expanded version in the Vashon-Maury Island Beachcomber in 1967. Her work preserved the oral histories and pioneer stories that might otherwise have been lost, forming a foundation for later historians. historian

records.title: Bill Moyer
records.text: Bill Moyer Fourth-generation Washingtonian and Vashon Island resident who founded the Backbone Campaign in 2003. Pioneered 'artful activism' combining creative arts with environmental and social justice advocacy. Led campaigns including opposition to Lower Snake River dams for salmon and orca protection. His annual Action Camp on Vashon became a national model for activist training. community leader

records.title: Alfred J. Stuckey
records.text: Alfred J. Stuckey Superintendent of the Martinolich Shipyard (Dockton Dry Dock) on Quartermaster Harbor from its founding through 1909. Oversaw construction of numerous vessels including steam launches and small freighters. Under his management, the yard employed over 80 workers and became one of the most important maritime industrial operations on Puget Sound. business owner

records.title: John A. Martinolich
records.text: John A. Martinolich Croatian-born shipbuilder known as the 'King of Purse Seiners' in the 1920s. Operated the Martinolich Shipyard at Dockton on Quartermaster Harbor, building and repairing vessels for the Puget Sound fishing fleet. His yard attracted a community of Croatian workers, creating a distinctive ethnic enclave at Dockton that influenced the island's cultural diversity. business owner

records.title: Mary Bridges
records.text: Mary Bridges Wife of Mathew Bridges, the first European-American homesteader on Vashon Island (1865). Believed to have been of Duwamish descent, representing one of the earliest examples of intermarriage between settlers and indigenous peoples on the island. Her presence highlights the complex relationships between indigenous and settler communities in the earliest days of homesteading. historical figure

records.title: Homer Hadley
records.text: Homer Hadley Engineer and bridge designer who proposed a cross-sound bridge connecting Vashon Island to the mainland in the 1930s. Known for designing the Mercer Island floating bridge (Lacey V. Murrow Memorial Bridge). His Vashon bridge proposal sparked decades of debate about the island's future character — whether to remain ferry-dependent and rural or become connected and suburban. historical figure

records.title: Sakai Family
records.text: Sakai Family One of several prominent Japanese American farming families on Vashon Island who cultivated strawberries and other crops from the early 1900s through 1942. Like the Mukai and Matsuda families, the Sakais were forcibly removed during Executive Order 9066 and sent to internment camps. Their farms were never fully recovered after the war. farmer

records.title: Hoshi Family
records.text: Hoshi Family Japanese American farming family on Vashon Island who were part of the thriving agricultural community that made the island one of the leading strawberry producers in Washington state. Forcibly removed during the 1942 internment of Japanese Americans, their story is part of the broader narrative of loss and resilience that shaped the island's WWII history. farmer

records.title: Bill Knox
records.text: Bill Knox Vashon-based artist, designer, and engineer who created the iconic color schemes for K2 skis and built the original prototype for the K2 ski boot. As a painter he specialized in watercolor landscapes and wildlife, with work selected for U.S. postage stamps. His combination of artistic talent and engineering skill was central to K2's distinctive visual identity during its growth years. artist

records.title: Peter Manson
records.text: Peter Manson Named the village of Dockton on Quartermaster Harbor, noting the dry dock facility could 'dock a ton of boats.' Later founded a pile driving company that became Manson Construction, which grew into a major marine construction firm that still operates today. His entrepreneurship at Dockton exemplified the industrial ambition that characterized Vashon's growth era. business owner

records.title: August M. Takatsuka
records.text: August M. Takatsuka Vashon-born son of Japanese immigrant farmers who returned from military service in WWII to resume strawberry farming on the island. Later transitioned to Christmas tree cultivation in the 1970s. His persistence in farming after the devastation of internment represented the resilience of the Japanese American agricultural community on Vashon. farmer

records.title: Sato Mukai
records.text: Sato Mukai First wife of Denichiro Mukai, who died in 1921. Her death preceded the family's land purchase in their American-born son Masa's name in 1926, a legal strategy necessitated by the Washington State Alien Land Law that barred Japanese immigrants from owning property. historical figure

records.title: Suquamish
records.text: Suquamish Coast Salish people whose traditional territory included the western shores of Puget Sound. The Suquamish made seasonal use of Vashon Island for fishing, hunting, and gathering, and participated in extensive trade networks with neighboring tribes. indigenous people

records.title: Puyallup
records.text: Puyallup Coast Salish people of southern Puget Sound. The Puyallup traded extensively with other tribes across the Sound, including through waterways adjacent to Vashon Island. Today, the Puyallup Tribe of Indians includes enrolled descendants of the S'Homamish who inhabited Vashon Island. indigenous people

records.title: Nisqually
records.text: Nisqually Coast Salish people whose traditional territory centered on the Nisqually River delta in southern Puget Sound. The Nisqually participated in regional trade networks that connected communities across the Sound, including those around Vashon Island. indigenous people

records.title: Duwamish
records.text: Duwamish Coast Salish people of the central Puget Sound whose traditional territory included the Duwamish River and Elliott Bay area (modern Seattle). The Duwamish traded with neighboring peoples across the Sound and shared cultural and kinship ties with the S'Homamish of Vashon Island. indigenous people

records.title: Chief Si'ahl
records.text: Chief Si'ahl Leader of the Duwamish and Suquamish peoples, for whom the city of Seattle is named. Known for his eloquent speeches about the relationship between indigenous peoples and settlers. indigenous leader

records.title: Arthur A. Denny
records.text: Arthur A. Denny Leader of the Denny Party, the founding settlers of Seattle. Arrived at Alki Point in November 1851 and helped establish the city. settler / city founder

records.title: David Denny
records.text: David Denny Member of the Denny Party and younger brother of Arthur A. Denny. Among the first settlers at Alki Point in 1851. settler

records.title: Doc Maynard
records.text: Doc Maynard David Swinson 'Doc' Maynard, early Seattle settler and physician who advocated for friendly relations with Native peoples and helped name the city after Chief Si'ahl. settler / physician

records.title: Robert Moran
records.text: Robert Moran Seattle mayor during the Great Fire of 1889 who led rebuilding efforts. Later became a shipbuilder and industrialist. mayor / industrialist

records.title: David E. Skinner
records.text: David E. Skinner Seattle shipping magnate who helped develop Harbor Island and expanded Seattle's shipbuilding capacity during World War I. shipping executive

records.title: Anna Louise Strong
records.text: Anna Louise Strong Seattle labor activist, journalist, and radical who supported the 1919 Seattle General Strike through her writing in the Union Record. journalist / activist

records.title: Ole Hanson
records.text: Ole Hanson Mayor of Seattle during the 1919 General Strike who took a hard line against the strikers, gaining national attention. mayor

records.title: Arthur Langlie
records.text: Arthur Langlie Governor of Washington State who oversaw the creation of Washington State Ferries in 1951, transitioning Puget Sound ferry service to state operation. governor

records.title: Bill Gates
records.text: Bill Gates Co-founder of Microsoft Corporation, which moved to the Puget Sound region in 1979 and transformed the area into a global technology hub. technology entrepreneur

records.title: Paul Allen
records.text: Paul Allen Co-founder of Microsoft Corporation alongside Bill Gates. Major philanthropist and investor in the Seattle area. technology entrepreneur

records.title: Jeff Bezos
records.text: Jeff Bezos Founder of Amazon.com, which started in Bellevue in 1994 and grew to become one of the world's largest companies, reshaping Seattle's economy and skyline. technology entrepreneur

records.title: Charles Enoch Peabody
records.text: Charles Enoch Peabody Captain and executive of the Puget Sound Navigation Company who consolidated the Mosquito Fleet into a dominant ferry operation serving Puget Sound. ferry company executive

records.title: James Colman
records.text: James Colman Scottish-born engineer and businessman who built Colman Dock in 1882, establishing Seattle's primary waterfront ferry terminal. engineer / businessman

records.title: Jacob Weisbach
records.text: Jacob Weisbach Mayor of Tacoma during the 1885 anti-Chinese expulsion, who facilitated the forced removal of Chinese residents from the city. mayor

records.title: Chauncey Griggs
records.text: Chauncey Griggs Co-founder of the St. Paul & Tacoma Lumber Company in 1888, one of the largest lumber operations in the Pacific Northwest. lumber industrialist

records.title: Henry Hewitt Jr.
records.text: Henry Hewitt Jr. Co-founder of the St. Paul & Tacoma Lumber Company and prominent Tacoma business leader in the late 19th century. lumber industrialist

records.title: Frederick Weyerhaeuser
records.text: Frederick Weyerhaeuser Timber magnate who incorporated the Weyerhaeuser Timber Company in Tacoma in 1900 after purchasing 900,000 acres of Pacific Northwest timberland. timber industrialist

records.title: James J. Hill
records.text: James J. Hill Railroad magnate known as the 'Empire Builder' who sold 900,000 acres of Northern Pacific land to Frederick Weyerhaeuser, enabling the Weyerhaeuser Timber Company. railroad magnate

records.title: Leonard Coatsworth
records.text: Leonard Coatsworth Tacoma News Tribune editor who was the last person to drive across the Tacoma Narrows Bridge before its dramatic collapse on November 7, 1940. newspaper editor

records.title: Mixie Green
records.text: Mixie Green Mixie is the heart of Whispering Pines — a bartender whose warmth masks a deeper unease. She is writing a novel about a bartender in a time-shifting lodge, unaware that identical drafts exist from the 1930s and 1940s. She remembers every drink she has ever poured but cannot remember why she started. Head Bartender

records.title: Flynn Callahan
records.text: Flynn Callahan Mixie's partner behind the bar — steady, warm, deeply protective. Lives in Owl cabin. Repairs watches as meditation. Callahan name appears in the Foresters' 1935 membership ledger. Co-Bartender

records.title: Siobhan Ni Ceallaigh (The Woman of the Storm)
records.text: Siobhan Ni Ceallaigh (The Woman of the Storm) Born County Kerry ~1889, arrived 1912 with husband Cormac. After Cormac was lost at sea in 1915, her grief-fueled ritual in Room 33 transformed it into a threshold between times. She did not die conventionally — she became part of the lodge. Origin Figure / Supernatural Presence

records.title: Chris Willis
records.text: Chris Willis 54-year-old cynic, Triangle Bar's most reliable presence. Vanishes during mid-season storm and returns with no memory of where he went. Bar Regular

records.title: Zahra "Z" Miranzadeh
records.text: Zahra "Z" Miranzadeh High-powered venture capital partner who arrives between deals. The lodge forces her to slow down. Her organizational instincts help decode the Foresters' structure. Venture Capital Partner

records.title: Marie Dorion
records.text: Marie Dorion 67-year-old cultural steward with deep Indigenous roots. Provides perspective the Foresters' records lack — land was a place of passage requiring relationship, not control. Cultural Steward / Lodge Regular

records.title: Matt Carlson
records.text: Matt Carlson Warm, genuine guest. First Season One test subject for Room 33. Enters Episode 4 and emerges changed. Recurring Guest

records.title: Sam Taylor
records.text: Sam Taylor 44-year-old environmental scientist studying anomalous weather. Instruments detect impossibilities — barometric, electromagnetic, and statistical correlation connecting Room 33 to disappearances. Environmental Scientist

records.title: Akira Yang
records.text: Akira Yang 26-year-old fashion designer whose entire life is curated performance. The lodge strips away the aesthetic layer by layer. Fashion Designer

records.title: Stefan Shooter
records.text: Stefan Shooter AR engineer whose worldview is that reality can be enhanced, measured, and controlled. The lodge disassembles this belief. A library book that describes events before they happen cracks his empiricism. AR Engineer

records.title: Esmerelda
records.text: Esmerelda 59-year-old astrologer and medium who has been visiting the lodge for years. Senses what others cannot. Whispers a blessing as Mixie leaves for Room 33. Astrologer and Medium

records.title: Tom Hargrove
records.text: Tom Hargrove 63-year-old groundskeeper whose actual tenure may be far longer than records show. Maintains the boiler, the hatch to the caves, and both the mechanical and supernatural systems of the lodge. His vigil speech is the series' emotional bedrock. Groundskeeper

records.title: Jauncey Pladiym
records.text: Jauncey Pladiym 63-year-old folk singer, Triangle Bar fixture for decades. Plays, listens, remembers. Has knowledge of the Foresters from years of listening. An original song in the finale is Season One's musical resolution. Folk Singer

records.title: The Mirror
records.text: The Mirror Antique mirror at the Triangle Bar entry that reflects everything a fraction late. The most public supernatural feature of the lodge. Shows reflections from other eras. In Episode 9, serves as the medium for Mixie to see Siobhan. Supernatural Entity

records.title: Dr. Aldric Voss
records.text: Dr. Aldric Voss Founder of the Foresters of the Eternal Compass. Arrived at the lodge in 1928, obsessed with understanding and controlling its threshold properties. His hubris led to the society's destruction when he carried something from the Water Chamber into Room 33 in 1943. Antagonist / Foresters Founder

records.title: M. Quinn
records.text: M. Quinn A woman who tended bar at the Triangle from 1935 to 1942. She looked exactly like Mixie Green and wrote an identical novel. Her identity is the central mystery of the cycle — was she Mixie in another era, or a previous iteration of the same pattern? Bartender / Mystery Figure

records.title: Iris Malone
records.text: Iris Malone Identified by the Foresters as an 'Anomaly' — a guest with unusual sensitivity to the lodge's threshold properties. She disappeared in 1938, a victim of the Foresters' increasingly dangerous experiments with Room 33. Vanished Guest / Foresters Victim

records.title: Vivian Cross
records.text: Vivian Cross Another woman who looked like Mixie, tending bar at the Triangle during the 1950s. Her existence confirms the cycle — the lodge perpetually draws a version of the same bartender-witness across eras. Bartender / Cycle Figure

records.title: Harold Fink
records.text: Harold Fink A guest who opened Room 33 during a storm in 1967. What he saw was never recorded — only that he screamed. The incident led to Room 33 being sealed, its compass rose papered over, and its existence suppressed by management. Witness / Catalyst

records.title: Alki Point
records.text: Alki Point Landing site of the Denny Party in 1851, the founding settlement of what would become Seattle. Located on the western shore of Elliott Bay.

records.title: Duwamish River
records.text: Duwamish River River flowing into Elliott Bay, central to Duwamish tribal life and later industrialized as part of Seattle's harbor development.

records.title: Pioneer Square
records.text: Pioneer Square Seattle's oldest neighborhood, devastated by the Great Fire of 1889 and rebuilt in brick and stone. The heart of early Seattle.

records.title: Pike Place Market
records.text: Pike Place Market Seattle's iconic public farmers market, opened in 1907 to connect consumers directly with farmers. One of the oldest continuously operated public markets in the U.S.

records.title: Harbor Island
records.text: Harbor Island Artificial island at the mouth of the Duwamish River, created in the early 1900s and developed into a major shipbuilding and industrial center.

records.title: Boeing Plant 2
records.text: Boeing Plant 2 Boeing's massive wartime factory along the Duwamish River where B-17 and B-29 bombers were produced during World War II.

records.title: Colman Dock
records.text: Colman Dock Seattle's primary waterfront ferry terminal, built by James Colman in 1882. Served as the hub for Puget Sound ferry service for over a century.

records.title: Seattle Center
records.text: Seattle Center 74-acre civic campus built for the 1962 Century 21 Exposition (Seattle World's Fair). Home to the Space Needle, museums, and performance venues.

records.title: Space Needle
records.text: Space Needle 605-foot observation tower built for the 1962 World's Fair, Seattle's most iconic architectural landmark.

records.title: Bellevue
records.text: Bellevue City east of Seattle across Lake Washington. Became a major technology hub after Microsoft moved there in 1979.

records.title: Redmond
records.text: Redmond City east of Bellevue that became Microsoft's permanent headquarters location, transforming from a rural community to a tech center.

records.title: Medicine Creek
records.text: Medicine Creek Creek near present-day Olympia where the 1854 Treaty of Medicine Creek was signed, ceding tribal lands including Vashon Island to the U.S. government.

records.title: Point Defiance Park
records.text: Point Defiance Park 760-acre park at the northern tip of Tacoma overlooking Puget Sound and Vashon Island, established in 1888. Site of the Tahlequah ferry terminal.

records.title: Ruston
records.text: Ruston Small city adjacent to Tacoma, site of the ASARCO copper smelter that operated from 1889 to 1985. Smelter emissions affected Vashon Island for decades.

records.title: Stadium High School
records.text: Stadium High School Tacoma landmark originally built as a luxury hotel in 1891, converted to a high school in 1906 after a fire. Notable for its French chateau-style architecture.

records.title: Tacoma Narrows
records.text: Tacoma Narrows Strait connecting the main basin of Puget Sound with its southern reaches, between Tacoma and the Kitsap Peninsula. Site of the famous bridge collapse of 1940.

records.title: Puyallup
records.text: Puyallup City southeast of Tacoma, home to the Puyallup Tribe and site of the Western Washington Fairgrounds used as Camp Harmony internment assembly center in 1942.

records.title: Puyallup Fairgrounds
records.text: Puyallup Fairgrounds Western Washington Fairgrounds in Puyallup, used as 'Camp Harmony' temporary assembly center where Japanese Americans were detained in 1942 before transfer to permanent internment camps.

records.title: Tacoma Dome
records.text: Tacoma Dome Large wooden-domed arena in Tacoma, opened in 1983. One of the largest wood-domed structures in the world.

records.title: Whispering Pines Lodge
records.text: Whispering Pines Lodge A remote Pacific Northwest lodge on Vashon Island where time moves differently. Built 1910, renovated 1935 by Foresters, operating continuously.

records.title: Room 33
records.text: Room 33 The threshold room at the lodge's heart. Created by Siobhan's 1915 ritual. Guests during storms may emerge transformed, terrified, or not at all.

records.title: The Triangle Bar
records.text: The Triangle Bar Emotional center — triangular room where Mixie and Flynn tend bar. Every confession, relationship, and story passes through.

records.title: The Great Room
records.text: The Great Room Lodge's communal center with massive stone fireplace burning continuously since 1910. Fire's ash contains objects from other eras, collected by Tom.

records.title: The Lobby & Front Desk
records.text: The Lobby & Front Desk Illusion of normalcy — competent hotel lobby masking lodge's true nature. Guest ledger contains every name since 1910.

records.title: The Library
records.text: The Library Wood-paneled room with ~2,000 books, Foresters' coded texts, clock synced to boiler. Locked cabinet contains Foresters' records and earlier drafts of Mixie's novel.

records.title: The Dining Room & Kitchen
records.text: The Dining Room & Kitchen Lodge's most practical spaces — grounding supernatural in ordinary. Kitchen resists supernatural influence. Communal table since 1910.

records.title: The Service Corridors
records.text: The Service Corridors Network of narrow passages. Sound travels impossibly. During storms, carry whispers from other eras and rearrange spatially.

records.title: The Basement & Boiler Room
records.text: The Basement & Boiler Room Tom's domain. 1935 Kewanee steam boiler modified by Foresters. Concealed hatch to cave system. Boiler accelerates before storms. Steam visions form.

records.title: The Storage Rooms (Lost and Found)
records.text: The Storage Rooms (Lost and Found) Off service corridors — belongings left by guests who vanished. Tom maintains it like a cemetery. Locked Voss steamer trunk is Season Two mystery.

records.title: The Whispering Pines (Forest)
records.text: The Whispering Pines (Forest) Old-growth Pacific Northwest rainforest surrounding lodge. Trees produce sustained whisper. Trails shift during storms. Forest is lodge's soft boundary.

records.title: The Clearing & Fire Pit
records.text: The Clearing & Fire Pit Natural clearing quarter mile south with fire pit ringed by river stones predating European settlement. Lodge's outdoor confessional.

records.title: The Stone Circle
records.text: The Stone Circle Twelve glacial erratics in circle deep in forest, thirteenth at center. Oldest intentional structure. Moss grows to perimeter but does not cross.

records.title: The Guest Cabins
records.text: The Guest Cabins Six detached cabins along Shore Path, each with own personality. They drift — shifting position subtly. Named: Cedar, Fern, Owl, Hemlock, Raven, Moss. Owl is Flynn's. Moss retains Siobhan's lavender.

records.title: The Caves
records.text: The Caves Branching cave system beneath lodge — oldest space. Three levels: Upper Chambers, Middle Passages, Water Chamber with temporally reflective pool. Deeper you go, less stable time becomes.

records.title: The Subterranean Waterways
records.text: The Subterranean Waterways Underground streams threading cave system — lodge's connective tissue. Water carries temporal and memorial properties. Spring emerges in basement at constant 42 degrees. Water is memory.

records.title: The Hidden Rooms
records.text: The Hidden Rooms Spaces appearing only when conditions are met — during storms, for specific people, at specific emotional states. Known rooms: Writing Room, Memory Room, Mirror Room, Seventh Cabin.

records.title: The Shore Path
records.text: The Shore Path Path connecting the guest cabins along the shoreline, serving as the lodge's edge where forest meets water. The boundary between the lodge's domain and the wider island.
